blocks.text: The **19th-century reform movements** — the **'Indian Renaissance'** — combined colonial modernity with indigenous revival to attack **sati, caste, untouchability, child marriage and superstition** and to promote **women's rights and education**. They span **reformist (Brahmo) and revivalist (Arya Samaj)** streams, with a strong **Andhra** chapter (Veeresalingam).

rows: **Raja Ram Mohan Roy** — monotheism, anti-sati (banned 1829), women's rights; 'father of Indian Renaissance'.
**Swami Dayananda Saraswati** — 'Back to the Vedas', **Shuddhi**, anti-idolatry, DAV schools.
**Sir Syed Ahmad Khan** — Muslim modern education (MAO College).
**Prarthana Samaj, Satyashodhak Samaj (Jyotiba Phule), Theosophical Society (Annie Besant), SNDP (Narayana Guru)**.
**Kandukuri Veeresalingam** — 'father of Telugu Renaissance'; widow remarriage, women's education, anti-nautch.

items: Reformist (Brahmo — Roy) vs revivalist (Arya Samaj — Dayananda) is the key split.
Andhra: Veeresalingam = Telugu Renaissance (widow remarriage) — always cite for AP.

prelimsPointers: **Raja Ram Mohan Roy** — **Brahmo Samaj (1828)**; campaigned to abolish **Sati (banned 1829)**; 'father of Indian Renaissance'.
**Dayananda Saraswati** — **Arya Samaj (1875)**; slogan **'Back to the Vedas'**; **Shuddhi** movement; DAV schools.
**Vivekananda** — **Ramakrishna Mission (1897)**; Chicago Parliament of Religions (1893).
**Jyotiba Phule** — Satyashodhak Samaj; **Sir Syed Ahmad Khan** — Aligarh (MAO College).
**Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar** — Widow Remarriage Act (1856); women's education (Bengal).
**Kandukuri Veeresalingam** — 'father of Telugu Renaissance'; **widow remarriage in Andhra**, girls' education, anti-nautch.
**Gurajada Appa Rao** ('Kanyasulkam') & **Raghupathi Venkataratnam Naidu** — Andhra social reformers.
mainsAngles: Assess the socio-religious reform movements as the making of modern India (and Andhra).

glossary.definition: Ram Mohan Roy's 1828 reform society advocating monotheism and social reform.
The Arya Samaj's movement to reconvert/purify people back into the Hindu fold.
Kandukuri Veeresalingam, the 'father of the Telugu Renaissance' and pioneer of widow remarriage in Andhra.

blocks.text: India's freedom struggle (**1885–1947**) evolved through distinct phases — from **Moderate constitutionalism to Extremist assertion, Gandhian mass movements, and the final transfer of power** — around the **Indian National Congress (founded 1885)**.

rows: **A.O. Hume** founds INC (1885); prayer-petition-protest; **Dadabhai Naoroji, Gokhale, Pherozeshah Mehta, Ranade**.
**Swadeshi** (Bengal partition 1905); **Lal-Bal-Pal**; Surat Split (1907); Home Rule (1916, Tilak & Besant).
**Non-Cooperation (1920), Civil Disobedience (1930), Quit India (1942)**; mass satyagraha.
**INA, RIN Mutiny, Cabinet Mission, Mountbatten Plan, Independence & Partition (15 Aug 1947)**.

items: INC founded 1885 (A.O. Hume, first session Bombay, W.C. Bonnerjee).
Phase markers: Swadeshi 1905, Surat Split 1907, NCM 1920, CDM 1930, Quit India 1942.

prelimsPointers: **INC founded 1885** by **A.O. Hume**; first session **Bombay**, president **W.C. Bonnerjee**.
**Moderates** — Naoroji (drain theory), **Gokhale (Gandhi's mentor)**, Pherozeshah Mehta, Ranade.
**Extremists** — **Lal-Bal-Pal** (Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal); **Tilak — 'Swaraj is my birthright'**.
**Swadeshi & Boycott** launched against the **Partition of Bengal (1905)**.
**Surat Split (1907)** — Congress divided into Moderates & Extremists.
**Home Rule Leagues (1916)** — **Tilak & Annie Besant**.
Gandhian mass movements — **NCM (1920), CDM (1930), Quit India (1942)**.
mainsAngles: Trace the evolution of the national movement from Moderate to Gandhian phases.

glossary.definition: The early INC leaders (1885-1905) who used constitutional 'prayer, petition, protest'.
The assertive nationalists (Lal-Bal-Pal) who demanded Swaraj and used Swadeshi/boycott.
The 1907 division of the Congress into Moderate and Extremist factions.

blocks.text: Alongside constitutional struggle ran a **revolutionary (militant) nationalism** — secret societies and armed action at home and abroad — from **Anushilan Samiti and the HSRA (Bhagat Singh) to the Ghadar Party and the Berlin Committee** — that kept the flame of radical patriotism alive.

rows: **Anushilan Samiti, Jugantar; Chapekar brothers; Khudiram Bose & Prafulla Chaki (Muzaffarpur 1908)**.
**Kakori (1925, Ram Prasad Bismil, Ashfaqullah)**; **HSRA (1928)** — **Bhagat Singh, Rajguru, Sukhdev, Chandrashekhar Azad**; Assembly bomb (1929); Lahore Conspiracy (Saunders).
**Ghadar Party (1913, San Francisco — Lala Har Dayal, Sohan Singh Bhakna); India House (London — Shyamji Krishna Varma, Savarkar); Berlin Committee; Madam Cama** (flag at Stuttgart 1907).
**Alluri Sitarama Raju** — Rampa (Manyam) Rebellion (1922-24), Godavari agency.

items: HSRA (Bhagat Singh, Azad); Kakori 1925; Ghadar Party 1913 (San Francisco).
Andhra: Alluri Sitarama Raju's Rampa Rebellion — always cite for AP.

prelimsPointers: **Khudiram Bose & Prafulla Chaki** — Muzaffarpur bombing (1908).
**Kakori Conspiracy (1925)** — Ram Prasad Bismil, Ashfaqullah Khan, Rajendra Lahiri.
**HSRA (1928)** — **Bhagat Singh, Rajguru, Sukhdev, Chandrashekhar Azad**; killed **Saunders**; Assembly bomb (1929).
**Ghadar Party (1913, San Francisco)** — Lala Har Dayal, Sohan Singh Bhakna.
**Madam Bhikaji Cama** unfurled an early Indian flag at **Stuttgart (1907)**.
**India House (London)** — Shyamji Krishna Varma, V.D. Savarkar.
**Alluri Sitarama Raju** led the **Rampa/Manyam Rebellion (1922-24)** in the Godavari agency (AP).
mainsAngles: Evaluate the role of revolutionary nationalism in the freedom struggle.

glossary.definition: The Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (1928) of Bhagat Singh and Chandrashekhar Azad.
A 1913 revolutionary party of Indian émigrés founded in San Francisco.
The leader of the Rampa Rebellion (1922-24) in the Andhra Godavari agency.

blocks.text: **Mahatma Gandhi's** philosophy rested on **Satya (truth) and Ahimsa (non-violence)**, operationalised as **Satyagraha** — a moral force to resist injustice. His broader vision embraced **Sarvodaya, Swadeshi, trusteeship, and constructive work (Harijan uplift, khadi)**, making him the moral and mass leader of the freedom struggle.

rows: 'Truth-force' / 'soul-force' — non-violent resistance to injustice (first used in **South Africa**).
Non-violence in thought, word and deed — the core method.
'Welfare of all'; upliftment of the last person (**Antyodaya**); inspired by Ruskin's Unto This Last.
The wealthy hold wealth as trustees for society — a non-Marxist economic ethic.
Self-reliance; **charkha (spinning wheel)** as economic & symbolic self-rule.
Harijan (Dalit) uplift, Hindu-Muslim unity, prohibition, village self-sufficiency (Gram Swaraj).

items: Satya + Ahimsa → Satyagraha; Sarvodaya/Antyodaya; Trusteeship; Swadeshi/khadi; Gram Swaraj.
Key texts: Hind Swaraj (1909); influences — Tolstoy, Ruskin, Thoreau, Gita.

prelimsPointers: **Satyagraha** — 'truth/soul-force'; first evolved in **South Africa** (against apartheid laws).
Twin pillars — **Satya (truth) & Ahimsa (non-violence)**.
**Sarvodaya** ('welfare of all') & **Antyodaya** (rise of the last person).
**Trusteeship** — the rich as trustees of wealth for society.
**Hind Swaraj (1909)** — Gandhi's key ideological text; **Gram Swaraj** (village self-rule).
Influences — **Bhagavad Gita, Ruskin (Unto This Last), Tolstoy, Thoreau (civil disobedience), Jainism**.
Constructive work — **khadi/charkha, Harijan uplift, Hindu-Muslim unity, prohibition**.
mainsAngles: Examine the philosophical foundations of Gandhian thought and their relevance today.

glossary.definition: Gandhi's method of non-violent resistance based on truth and moral force.
Gandhi's ideal of the welfare and upliftment of all, especially the last person.
Gandhi's principle that the wealthy hold their wealth in trust for the benefit of society.

sections.heading: Champaran to Non-Cooperation — early Gandhian satyagrahas

blocks.text: Gandhi's Indian leadership began with three local **satyagrahas (1917–18) — Champaran, Ahmedabad, Kheda** — establishing his method, and rose to the first all-India mass movement, the **Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22)**, launched with the Khilafat cause and halted after **Chauri Chaura**.

rows: Bihar; indigo planters' **tinkathia** system; Gandhi's **first satyagraha in India** — success.
Gujarat peasants' revenue relief amid famine; **Sardar Patel** emerged.
Rowlatt Act protest; **Jallianwala Bagh massacre (13 Apr 1919, Gen. Dyer)**.
With **Khilafat**; boycott of titles/schools/courts/foreign goods; called off after **Chauri Chaura (Feb 1922)**.

items: Champaran (1917) = Gandhi's first Indian satyagraha; Ahmedabad = first fast; Kheda = Patel emerges.
NCM launched with Khilafat; withdrawn after Chauri Chaura (violence).

prelimsPointers: **Champaran (1917)** — Gandhi's **first satyagraha in India**; against the indigo **tinkathia** system (Bihar).
**Ahmedabad Mill Strike (1918)** — Gandhi's **first hunger strike**.
**Kheda satyagraha (1918)** — peasant revenue relief; **Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel** rose to prominence.
**Rowlatt Act (1919)** — 'no vakil, no appeal, no daleel'; sparked the **Jallianwala Bagh massacre (13 April 1919)** under **General Dyer**.
**Non-Cooperation Movement (1920)** — combined with the **Khilafat** movement (Ali brothers).
Programme — boycott of **titles, councils, schools, courts, foreign cloth**.
Withdrawn after the **Chauri Chaura incident (Feb 1922)** — a mob burned a police station.
mainsAngles: Discuss the significance of Gandhi's early satyagrahas and the Non-Cooperation Movement.

glossary.definition: The system forcing Champaran peasants to grow indigo on 3/20 of their land, challenged by Gandhi.
Gandhi's first all-India mass movement (1920-22), withdrawn after Chauri Chaura.
The February 1922 violent incident that led Gandhi to call off Non-Cooperation.
